title: Strings and the strings Package
summary: Index, slice, and join strings, then search, transform, split, and combine them with the strings package.
intro: A Go string is an immutable sequence of bytes. You can measure it, index it, and slice it with the same syntax as a slice, and the standard `strings` package covers searching, cleaning, splitting, and joining. This lesson keeps to plain ASCII text. The next lesson handles letters that take more than one byte.

steps.title: String basics
steps.body:
A string is a read-only run of bytes. `len(s)` counts **bytes**, and `s[i]` is one byte (a `uint8`), so it prints as a number. Convert it with `string(s[i])` to get a one-letter string back.

```go
word := "Go"
fmt.Println(len(word), word[0], string(word[0])) // 2 71 G
```

Slicing works as it does on slices: `s[a:b]` includes `a` and excludes `b`, and `s[a:]` runs to the end. An index at or past `len(s)` panics at run time. `+` joins strings and `s += "x"` appends to a variable.

In memory a string value is a small header: a pointer to the bytes and a length. Assigning a string copies only that header, never the bytes. Because strings are **immutable**, `s[0] = 'x'` does not compile. That is what makes sharing safe: `s[1:4]` builds a new header that points into the same bytes, with no copying. The flip side: a short slice of a huge string keeps all of its bytes in memory. `+` and `+=` leave the old bytes alone: they allocate a new string and copy both sides into it.

Gotcha: `string(n)` on an integer gives the character with that code, so `string(65)` is `"A"`, not `"65"`. Use `fmt.Sprintf("%d", n)` for the digits.

example.title: Gopher pieces
example.prompt: Measure, index, slice, and extend the string `Gopher`.
example.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	word := "Gopher"
	fmt.Println("length:", len(word))
	fmt.Println("byte 0:", word[0])
	fmt.Println("letter 0:", string(word[0]))
	fmt.Println("word[1:4]:", word[1:4])
	message := word + "s"
	message += " rule"
	fmt.Println("message:", message)
	fmt.Println("word:", word)
}
example.output:
length: 6
byte 0: 71
letter 0: G
word[1:4]: oph
message: Gophers rule
word: Gopher
example.explanation: `len(word)` is 6 because each ASCII letter is one byte. `word[0]` is the byte for G, which prints as 71, and `string(word[0])` turns it back into `"G"`. `word[1:4]` takes bytes 1, 2, and 3. `+` and `+=` build brand new strings, so `word` itself is still `Gopher` at the end.

practice.title: City pieces
practice.prompt:
Measure, index, slice, and extend the string `Lisbon`.

1. Keep the given `city := "Lisbon"` and the line that prints its length.
2. Print `byte 2:` followed by `city[2]`, then `letter 2:` followed by that byte as a string.
3. Print `city[3:]:` followed by the slice from index 3 to the end.
4. Build `message` as `"I love " + city`, append `"!"` with `+=`, and print it after `message:`.
5. Print `city:` followed by `city` to show it did not change.

Expected output:

```text
length: 6
byte 2: 115
letter 2: s
city[3:]: bon
message: I love Lisbon!
city: Lisbon
```
practice.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	city := "Lisbon"
	fmt.Println("length:", len(city))
	fmt.Println("byte 2:", city[2])
	fmt.Println("letter 2:", string(city[2]))
	fmt.Println("city[3:]:", city[3:])
	message := "I love " + city
	message += "!"
	fmt.Println("message:", message)
	fmt.Println("city:", city)
}

tests.output:
length: 6
byte 2: 115
letter 2: s
city[3:]: bon
message: I love Lisbon!
city: Lisbon

hints: `city[2]` is a byte, so `fmt.Println` shows it as a number.
Wrap the byte in `string(...)` to print it as a letter.
`city[3:]` runs from index 3 to the end.

steps.title: Searching
steps.body:
Add `"strings"` to your imports to use the package. Its search functions take the string first, then what to look for:

- `strings.Contains(s, sub)` reports whether `sub` appears anywhere.
- `strings.HasPrefix(s, p)` and `strings.HasSuffix(s, p)` check the start and the end.
- `strings.Index(s, sub)` is the byte index of the first match, or **-1** when it is missing.
- `strings.LastIndex(s, sub)` is the index of the last match.
- `strings.Count(s, sub)` counts matches that do not overlap.
- `strings.EqualFold(a, b)` compares two strings ignoring case.

```go
at := strings.Index(email, "@")
if at != -1 {
	fmt.Println(email[:at])
}
```

Pair `Index` with slicing to cut a string at a separator. Check for -1 first: if `at` is -1, `email[:at]` panics at run time. All of these searches are case sensitive, like `==`. Use `EqualFold` instead of lowering both sides when you only need to compare.

example.title: Inspect a file name
example.prompt: Search the file name `report_2024_final.pdf` with the strings package.
example.output:
contains 2024: true
prefix report: true
suffix .pdf: true
first _: 6
last _: 11
count _: 2
index of zip: -1
name: report
equal fold: true
example.explanation: The first `_` is at byte 6 and the last at byte 11, and there are 2 in total. `zip` never appears, so `Index` returns -1. Since the first `_` was found, `file[:first]` keeps everything before it. `EqualFold` treats `PDF` and `pdf` as equal.

practice.title: Inspect an email
practice.prompt:
Search the address `ada.lovelace@example.com` with the strings package.

1. Keep the given `email` and the `contains @:` line.
2. Print `prefix ada:` with `HasPrefix` and `suffix .org:` with `HasSuffix`.
3. Store `strings.Index(email, "@")` in `at` and print it after `first @:`.
4. Print `last .:` with `LastIndex`, `count .:` with `Count`, and `index of #:` with `Index` of `#`.
5. If `at` is not -1, print `user:` followed by `email[:at]`.
6. Print `equal fold:` with `strings.EqualFold("ADA", "ada")`.

Expected output:

```text
contains @: true
prefix ada: true
suffix .org: false
first @: 12
last .: 20
count .: 2
index of #: -1
user: ada.lovelace
equal fold: true
```

tests.output:
contains @: true
prefix ada: true
suffix .org: false
first @: 12
last .: 20
count .: 2
index of #: -1
user: ada.lovelace
equal fold: true

hints: Every call takes the string first: `strings.HasSuffix(email, ".org")`.
`strings.Index` returns -1 when the text is missing.

steps.title: Transforming
steps.body:
Strings never change, so every `strings` function returns a **new** string. Assign the result or it is lost: `strings.ToUpper(s)` on its own line does nothing useful.

- `strings.ToUpper(s)` and `strings.ToLower(s)` change case.
- `strings.TrimSpace(s)` drops whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines) from both ends.
- `strings.Trim(s, cutset)` drops any of the characters in `cutset` from both ends.
- `strings.TrimPrefix(s, p)` and `strings.TrimSuffix(s, p)` remove one exact string, once, if it is there.
- `strings.Replace(s, old, new, n)` replaces the first `n` matches, and a negative `n` such as -1 means all.
- `strings.ReplaceAll(s, old, new)` replaces every match.
- `strings.Repeat(s, n)` glues `n` copies together.

The classic gotcha: `Trim`'s second argument is a **set of characters**, not a word. `strings.Trim("gogopher go", "go")` strips every `g` and `o` from both ends until it reaches a character outside the set. When you mean one exact prefix or suffix, use `TrimPrefix` or `TrimSuffix`.

example.title: Clean a handle
example.prompt: Clean up a messy handle one step at a time, then compare Trim with TrimPrefix.
example.code:
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"strings"
)

func main() {
	raw := "  Go_Dev!!  "
	s := strings.TrimSpace(raw)
	fmt.Printf("%q\n", s)
	s = strings.Trim(s, "!")
	fmt.Printf("%q\n", s)
	s = strings.ToLower(s)
	fmt.Printf("%q\n", s)
	s = strings.ReplaceAll(s, "_", "-")
	fmt.Printf("%q\n", s)
	s = strings.TrimPrefix(s, "go")
	fmt.Printf("%q\n", s)
	fmt.Println(strings.Repeat("=", 10))
	fmt.Printf("%q\n", strings.Trim("gogopher go", "go"))
	fmt.Printf("%q\n", strings.TrimPrefix("gogopher go", "go"))
	fmt.Printf("raw is still %q\n", raw)
}
example.explanation: Each call returns a new string that is stored back in `s`, and `%q` shows the quotes so you can see the spaces. `Trim` with the set `go` eats `g`, `o`, `g`, `o` from the left, stops at `p`, then eats `o` and `g` from the right, leaving `"pher "`. `TrimPrefix` removes the exact text `go` once. `raw` never changed.

practice.title: Clean a product code
practice.prompt:
Clean up a messy product code one step at a time, then compare Trim with TrimPrefix.

1. Keep the given `TrimSpace` step and its print.
2. Trim every `#` from both ends of `s`, then make `s` upper case.
3. Replace only the first `-` with `_` using `strings.Replace` with a count of 1.
4. Remove the suffix `-ABC` with `TrimSuffix`.
5. Print `s` with `%q` after each of those four steps.
6. Print `strings.Repeat("*", 8)`, then print `strings.Trim("abcabc-cab", "abc")` and `strings.TrimPrefix("abcabc-cab", "abc")` with `%q`.
7. Keep the given last line that prints `code`.

Expected output:

```text
"sku-123-abc##"
"sku-123-abc"
"SKU-123-ABC"
"SKU_123-ABC"
"SKU_123"
********
"-"
"abc-cab"
code is still "  sku-123-abc##  "
```
practice.solution:
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"strings"
)

func main() {
	code := "  sku-123-abc##  "
	s := strings.TrimSpace(code)
	fmt.Printf("%q\n", s)
	s = strings.Trim(s, "#")
	fmt.Printf("%q\n", s)
	s = strings.ToUpper(s)
	fmt.Printf("%q\n", s)
	s = strings.Replace(s, "-", "_", 1)
	fmt.Printf("%q\n", s)
	s = strings.TrimSuffix(s, "-ABC")
	fmt.Printf("%q\n", s)
	fmt.Println(strings.Repeat("*", 8))
	fmt.Printf("%q\n", strings.Trim("abcabc-cab", "abc"))
	fmt.Printf("%q\n", strings.TrimPrefix("abcabc-cab", "abc"))
	fmt.Printf("code is still %q\n", code)
}
hints: The last argument of `strings.Replace` says how many matches to change.
The suffix is matched after upper casing, so remove `-ABC`, not `-abc`.

steps.title: Split, Fields, and Join
steps.body:
`strings.Split(s, sep)` cuts a string at every `sep` and returns a `[]string`, so `len` and `range` work on the result. Each part is a substring that shares the original bytes.

Every separator counts, so two in a row produce an **empty string** between them, and so does a separator at either end. Println would show that as a double space, which is easy to miss. Print the slice with `%q` instead: it quotes every part, so empty ones show up as `""`.

```go
fmt.Printf("%q\n", strings.Split("a,,b", ",")) // ["a" "" "b"]
```

`strings.Fields(s)` splits on any run of spaces, tabs, or newlines and ignores them at both ends, which is what you want for words. Watch the empty case: `strings.Split("", ",")` returns one empty string (length 1), while `strings.Fields("")` returns an empty slice (length 0).

`strings.Join(parts, sep)` goes the other way: it puts `sep` between the parts and returns one string.

example.title: Colors and words
example.prompt: Split a list of colors, compare Split with Fields, and join the colors back together.
example.output:
3 colors
0 red
1 green
2 blue
["a" "" "b"]
3 words: [go is fun]
1 0
red | green | blue
example.explanation: `Split` returns three parts, which `range` walks with their indexes. In `a,,b` the two commas have nothing between them, and `%q` shows that empty part as `""`. `Fields` ignores the extra spaces and finds 3 words. Splitting an empty string gives one empty part, Fields gives none. `Join` puts ` | ` between the colors.

practice.title: Dates and words
practice.prompt:
Split a date, rebuild it in a new order, and compare Split with Fields.

1. Keep the given lines that split `"2024-03-15"` on `-` and print the count.
2. Use `range` to print each index and part, separated by a space.
3. Join `parts[2]`, `parts[1]`, and `parts[0]` with `/` and print the result.
4. Print `strings.Split("x;;y;z", ";")` with `%q`.
5. Split `"  the quick  brown fox "` with `Fields` and print the count, the word `words:`, and the slice on one line.
6. Print `len(strings.Split("", "-"))` and `len(strings.Fields("   "))` on one line.

Expected output:

```text
3 parts
0 2024
1 03
2 15
15/03/2024
["x" "" "y" "z"]
4 words: [the quick brown fox]
1 0
```
hints: `for i, p := range parts` gives each index and part.
`Join` takes a `[]string`, so build one with the parts in the new order.
`Fields` of only spaces has no words, so its length is 0.

recap:
- `len(s)` counts bytes, `s[i]` is a byte that prints as a number, and `string(s[i])` turns it into a letter.
- `s[a:b]` shares the original bytes. A string value is just a pointer and a length.
- Strings are immutable: `+`, `+=`, and every `strings` function return a new string, so assign the result.
- Search with `Contains`, `HasPrefix`, `HasSuffix`, `Index`, `LastIndex`, and `Count`. `Index` returns -1 when missing.
- `EqualFold` compares ignoring case.
- Transform with `ToUpper`, `ToLower`, `TrimSpace`, `Replace`, `ReplaceAll`, and `Repeat`.
- `Trim` removes a set of characters, while `TrimPrefix` and `TrimSuffix` remove one exact string.
- `Split` keeps empty parts (print with `%q` to see them), `Fields` splits on runs of whitespace, and `Join` glues parts back together.
- `Split` of an empty string has length 1, `Fields` of it has length 0.
